L8@P0: Abstract. Formal methods have proved effective to automatically analyze protocols. Over the past years, much research has focused on verifying trace equivalence on protocols, which is notably used to model many interesting privacy
L9@P0: properties, e.g., anonymity or unlinkability. Many tools for checking trace equivalence rely on a naive and expensive exploration of all interleavings of concurrent
L10@P0: actions, which calls for partial-order reduction (POR) techniques. In this paper,
L11@P0: we present the first POR technique for protocol equivalences that does not rely on
L12@P0: an action-determinism assumption: we recast the trace equivalence problem as a
L13@P0: reachability problem, to which persistent and sleep set techniques can be applied,
L14@P0: and we show how to effectively apply these results in the context of symbolic executions. We report on a prototype implementation, improving the tool DeepSec.
L15@P0: 1 Introduction
L16@P0: Security protocols are notoriously difficult to design, and their flaws can have a huge
L17@P0: impact. Leaving aside implementation flaws and weaknesses of cryptographic primitives, there is already a long history of logical mistakes in the basic design of protocols,
L18@P0: e.g., [28,6,12,5]. At this level of detail, protocols can however be represented in the socalled symbolic model, which makes them amenable to automated formal verification.
L19@P0: This approach has lead to mature tools and industrial successes, e.g., [13,7,29].
L20@P0: Verification techniques have focused at first on reachability properties of protocols,
L21@P0: used to model, e.g., the secrecy or authenticity or messages. More recently, equivalence
L22@P0: properties have received a lot of attention, as they are often necessary to model privacy
L23@P0: properties such as ballot secrecy in e-voting [23], anonymity or unlinkability [5,14].

L40@P1: All the techniques mentioned above for deciding trace equivalence of security protocols rely on an enumeration of all symbolic executions including all interleavings
L41@P1: of concurrent actions. This is obviously a cause of major inefficiency, which has lead
L42@P1: to the quest for partial-order reduction (POR) techniques. These techniques, which
L43@P1: have a long and successful history in traditional software verification [26,31,10], generally consist in leveraging action independencies to restrict the interleavings that a
L44@P1: model-checking algorithm explores. In the context of verifying reachability properties
L45@P1: for security protocols, some specific POR techniques have sometimes had to be devised [20,30], but there have also been successful uses of generic POR techniques such
L46@P1: as sleep sets [21] (see [9] for a detailed discussion). In the context of verifying equivalences for security protocols, the only available POR techniques are, to the best of our
L47@P1: knowledge, the ones we proposed in [8,9]. These ad hoc techniques have lead to significant performance gains in Apte and DeepSec [19,9]. However, they crucially rely
L48@P1: on an action-determinism assumption (i.e., once the observable trace is fixed, the system is deterministic) which is very limiting in practice. For instance, there is no precise
L49@P1: modeling of unlinkability involving action-deterministic systems.
L50@P1: In this paper, we present the first POR technique for checking trace equivalence on
L51@P1: security protocols, without any action-determinism assumption. Our first step towards
L52@P1: this goal is to recast the trace equivalence problem as a reachability problem in a carefully designed labeled transition system (LTS), to which we can then apply persistent
L53@P1: and sleep set techniques. However, this result is not directly useful in practice, for several reasons. First, this LTS is infinitely branching, due to the arbitrary choices that the
L54@P1: attacker can make when interacting with the protocol. This is the main issue addressed
L55@P1: in protocol equivalence checkers, typically through symbolic execution. Second, determining when two actions are independent (the first ingredient of POR techniques) is far
L56@P1: from obvious in our LTS. Independencies are often approximated through simple static
L57@P1: checks in practical POR algorithms [26] but, as we shall see, it does not seem feasible
L58@P1: in our setting without losing too many independencies. Instead, we determine independencies by exploring symbolic executions. We ignore constraint solving in that process,
L59@P1: as it would be too expensive: this trade-off allows us to detect enough independencies
L60@P1: at a reasonable cost. More generally, we show how to compute persistent sets in the
L61@P1: same style, to eventually obtain a symbolic form of the sleep set technique. Third, the
L62@P1: direct symbolic approach would still be overly expensive, due to another typical state
L63@P1: explosion problem caused by conditionals [11]. We circumvent it by showing that conditionals can be simplified, and often eliminated, in a way that does not affect persistent
L64@P1: set computations. This approach yields a POR technique that is fast enough and allows
L65@P1-2: to significantly reduce the number of symbolic traces to consider when checking equiv2alences. The technique is also independent of the specific verification algorithms that
L66@P2: will be used to check equivalence along the reduced set of traces. We implement it as a
L67@P2: library, and integrate it in DeepSec to validate the approach experimentally.
L68@P2: Outline. We present a standard security protocol model in Section 2. After recalling
L69@P2: persistent and sleep set techniques in Section 3, we design in Section 4 our concrete
L70@P2: equivalence LTS to which they apply. Section 5 then defines a symbolic abstraction of
L71@P2: this LTS, and shows how it can be used to obtain effective POR algorithms, notably
L72@P2: through the collapse of conditionals. Finally, we present our implementations and experimental results in Section 6. Detailed proofs and additional examples are given in
